rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry can serve tribal and poetic self-assertion, yet its intertwined vices outweigh its benefit; Islahi directs readers to his al-Baqarah discussion.
rows.anchor: means of expressing superiority to other tribes and poets, and even then such evils are intertwined with them that their harm surpasses their benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet's following gathers around him because their habits and traits resemble his.
rows.anchor: only those people will gather around a poet whose habits and traits are similar to him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wandering image marks purposeless compositions that voice every thought, whether divine, satanic, virtuous, vicious, or likely to move others toward good or evil.
rows.anchor: compositions of such poets have no purpose in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets shift between virtue and vice impulsively; their effective style influences readers, but the self inclines toward evil, so vice remains while good fades and any benefit is lost.
rows.anchor: one couplet will portray them a saint and another a devil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an has one coherent purpose served by every verse, contains no contradiction, and proves its purpose so persuasively that only an obdurate person can deny it; thus it is unlike poetry.
rows.anchor: From the beginning to the end every verse relates to this purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets claim heroic reputations but act shamefully, imagine rather than live their ideals, and may celebrate gallantry while being cowards.
rows.anchor: The ideals they present are never followed by them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet embodies the Book he presents, living its fear of God, selflessness, and altruism; even his strongest enemy cannot show a deviation between his beliefs and deeds and the Book.
rows.anchor: His strongest enemy cannot point out any deviation in his beliefs and deeds from the Book he is presenting.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception refers to poets in the Prophet's company, whose faith gives their poetry a defined purpose.
rows.anchor: Their faith has prescribed a purpose to their poetry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faithful poets write realistic poems that support and honor truth and seek to make God's word prevail.
rows.anchor: Their poems show support and express honour for the truth and are written to make the word of God superior.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike poets who merely posture, these poets manifest their stated qualities through piety and righteousness in their lives.
rows.anchor: These traits are manifested in their persons. Piety and righteousness are writ large in all their undertakings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their poetry centers on remembering God and advancing His word, without the love, lust, or mutual boasting common in other poetry.
rows.anchor: The content of their works mostly relates to God’s remembrance and in making His word prevail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When their poetry speaks of others, its aim is to defend truth after oppression rather than defame; the oppressed may defend themselves and people like them.
rows.anchor: Every oppressed person has the right to defend his own self and others like him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oppressed are defending themselves now, but their oppressors will soon encounter their fate.
rows.anchor: soon the time will come when they will encounter their fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic critique primarily targets pre-Qur'anic classical poetry but also applies to contemporary celebrated poets; Islahi says few meet its standards.
rows.anchor: Very few among them will conform to the standards presented by the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opposition should not distress the Prophet: the Qur'an comes from the wise and knowledgeable God, who will not forsake him and will guide him to his destination.
rows.anchor: This verse sounds an assurance to the Prophet (sws):

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section recounts God's granting Moses prophethood and sending him to Pharaoh and his people with nine miracles.
rows.anchor: In this section, that part of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses account reassures the Prophet that revelation is God's favor, just as God chose Moses, and shows opponents that prophethood is not strange or alien.
rows.anchor: Firstly, God has sent divine revelations to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those unwilling to believe remain blind even before miracles: Moses' audience saw nine signs of divine origin and still refused faith.
rows.anchor: Secondly, those who do not want to profess faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God necessarily seizes people who spread disorder after granting them a period of respite.
rows.anchor: Thirdly, the Almighty necessarily seizes people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Moses account has been explained in earlier sūrahs, Islahi focuses here on its coherence with the present sūrah.
rows.anchor: This account of Moses (sws) has been mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood is an uncommon, divinely selected task; those chosen for it need time to become accustomed to it.
rows.anchor: Only those people experience it who the Almighty selects for this special task.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The audience, too, finds prophethood unfamiliar and raises doubts and objections when it is presented.
rows.anchor: those before whom it was presented also regarded it to be something unique and strange

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stories of earlier prophets console the Prophet through their experience and observations, while presenting opponents with conclusive truth.
rows.anchor: so that the Prophet (sws) could find assurance and comfort through their experiences and observations and his rivals were also conveyed the truth in a conclusive way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses most resembles Muhammad; his life is detailed in the Torah, and the Israelites who claimed faith in Moses opposed Muhammad, making this account suited to reassure the Prophet and instruct his rivals.
rows.anchor: The prophet and messenger who resembled Mu ḥammad (sws) the most

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet is addressed in the story, its direction of address is toward his rivals.
rows.anchor: the direction of address is towards his rivals.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood and messengerhood are God's gift, not something a person can obtain by his own effort, unlike learned crafts and professions.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this verse that propehthood and messengerhood is a blessing and gift of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God trains and instructs prophets; they are not students of teachers or seminaries and do not seek appointment, but are prepared through trials and tests.
rows.anchor: God Himself trains and instructs a prophet and a messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's training in an Egyptian jail and Moses' service tending Jethro's goats in Midian exemplify God's preparation of prophets through their lives.
rows.anchor: Joseph (sws) was trained and instructed in a jail of Egypt.

rows.speaker: David (sws)
rows.claim: David is reported to have said that God took him from tending the flock and appointed him ruler over Israel.
rows.anchor: David (sws) is reported to have said about himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses tended Jethro's goats in Midian and, lost on a dark cold night while returning, saw a light and went seeking directions or an ember to warm his family.
rows.anchor: He lost his way on a dark and cold night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive verb leaves the caller and source of the voice ambiguous, while magnifying the event.
rows.anchor: The passive mood of the verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent fire is a veil of light behind which God's blessed being is with the blessed angels; it is not an ordinary fire.
rows.anchor: this is not fire: behind the veil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The announcement of blessing familiarizes and reassures Moses: an unexpected voice in the dark valley could frighten him, but its source and message signal no danger.
rows.anchor: this phase was very essential for Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glorification rules out false notions of God: He is free of defects, and Moses should trust His merciful providence, since the Lord of all worlds controls everything.
rows.anchor: God, Lord of the worlds, is free of all defects and shortcomings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God now addresses Moses directly and identifies Himself; Moses already knew these attributes, so their reminder is meant to strengthen his heart for the mission.
rows.anchor: to strengthen his heart for the mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the previous sūrah's repeated Powerful-Merciful pairing, this passage joins Powerful with Wise, emphasizing God's unopposable power and wisdom beyond all others.
rows.anchor: no one else has the extent of wisdom and knowledge as the one God has.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Understanding these attributes gives Moses determination to challenge Pharaoh alongside the Israelites, with God's help and support.
rows.anchor: determination and strength to challenge
